name: Blood Lantern
subtitle: an implant that glows when potassium climbs

effects.effect: a jellyfish protein makes any cell that carries its gene glow green
a learned model predicts a protein's 3D shape from its sequence

effect: a jellyfish protein makes any cell that carries its gene glow green
how: Kidney patients die suddenly in the days between dialysis sessions when potassium builds up and stops the heart, and the only way to know is a blood draw at a clinic. A speck of gel under the skin holds a designed glowing protein, built on the jellyfish one, that dims as potassium binds to it; a phone's lamp and camera read the brightness through the skin in a few seconds, as often as the patient likes.
obstacle: Skin tone, blood flow and the scar that forms around the implant all change the brightness, so the reading has to stay calibrated for a year.
why: Takes the one blood test dialysis patients cannot do at home and makes it hourly.
real: The pieces exist separately — fluoroionophore-based implanted potassium optical sensors are patented, fluorescent dermal tattoo sensors with crown-ether dyes are read transdermally by a smartphone plus filters, and a Fraunhofer/Ki'tech subcutaneous potassium monitor reached smartphone-readout proof of concept in 2025 — but no implanted engineered fluorescent protein potassium sensor read through the skin by phone camera was found.
